experimental warming in temperate grassland ecosystems lengthened growing seasons through earlier leaf emergence, but not reproductive seasons, and elevated CO2 further lengthened growing, but not the reproductive season, by conserving water and enabling plants to remain active longer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the response of plants to environmental change.
the response of plant life cycles to global change.
the effects of climate change on plant phenology, and the role of atmospheric CO2 in determining the length of the growing season.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
warming and elevated CO2 together extend the growing season in temperate grasslands, but warming alone may shorten the growing season.
warming alone does not lead to a longer growing period in all species and ecosystems, but elevated CO2 does.
the warming-induced lengthening of the growing season is a consequence of both warming and elevated CO2, and the latter effect is more pronounced in dry years and in dry biomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
elevated CO2 and warming can extend growing season length in temperate grasslands through the conservation of soil moisture.
warming and elevated CO2 have different and often counteracting effects on the length of the growing season.

elevated CO2 can extend growing season length, and that warming can extend growing season, but not reproductive season, length, and that the two together can lengthen both growing and reproductive season lengths.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the effect of elevated atmospheric CO2 on plant phenology is not limited to earlier leaf emergence and flowering, but also to delayed leaf senescence and seed maturation, and therefore to a longer active period of plant life cycles.
the effects of elevated CO2 on the growing season are more complex than expected and that warming and CO2 have opposing effects on the timing of plant phenology.

the length of the active period in annual plant life cycles, and the growing season, are determined by the balance between the timing and rate of leaf emergence and senescence, which are both influenced by climate warming and CO2 fertilization.
